#500. El Niño Is Driving a Record Marine Heat Wave Off the California Coast

For the past 20 years, Daniel Rudnick has been collecting data from below the ocean’s surface. He’s never seen anything like what’s been coming back for the past few months, as a super El Niño fuels record heat off the California coast. The marine heat wave is affecting wildlife and helping to juice the record-setting storms hitting the state at the start of the rainy season.

The oceanographer helps to pilot small underwater drones known as gliders that dive thousands of feet below the surface and crawl their way back up, collecting data on salinity, temperature, and other metrics.

A color-coded chart showing temperature anomalies at different depths in the ocean—red for hotter, blue for colder—had to be readjusted because the red shades weren’t intense enough to accurately reflect just how hot things are, even hundreds of meters below the surface. Steric height—changes to sea levels driven by heat rather than melting ice—has reached the highest levels Rudnick has ever seen.

“I looked back at our data to make sure that I'm not making a mistake and it's correct—and it is,” Rudnick, who works at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at UC San Diego, says.

In Monterey Bay, a station recorded a temperature of 64.72 degrees Fahrenheit (18.18 degrees Celsius) at a depth of 200 feet below the water’s surface in late October, breaking previous records. Other data shows even hotter water in San Diego at the same depth: 77 degrees Fahrenheit, an anomaly of 21.3 degrees Fahrenheit above normal.

El Niño “is the biggest source of climate variability” off the California coast, Rudnick says. The climate phenomenon is characterized by hotter-than-normal water in the eastern tropical Pacific and affects weather and oceans around the globe. His gliders have captured temperature anomalies across other events, including intense heat during the 2015–2016 super El Niño. But this year’s El Niño is shaping up to be the strongest on record, and its impacts are equally supersized.

“It’s fair to say it’s off the charts,” he says.

This year’s El Niño is adding heat to an already-simmering ocean. Since January 2025, coastal California waters have been hit by a massive heat wave, with temperatures in some places reaching 8 degrees Fahrenheit above average in August. Add in human-caused climate change—oceans off Southern California have warmed 1.8 degrees Fahrenheit since the 1970s alone—and it makes for unprecedented conditions now.

“This is a bunch of things that have had to come together to make this even physically possible,” Daniel Swain, a climate scientist at the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, says. “And even then, it's kind of astonishing.”

Rudnick agrees. “The heat we get from El Niño stacking on top of the heat we already have, that’s the thing that makes this most unusual,” he says.

Part of what’s driving the higher ocean temperatures and sea levels off California are what’s known as Kelvin waves. These slow, large waves transport warm water from west to east across the Pacific. They in turn push down the ocean’s thermocline, a transition layer into the deeper ocean where temperatures begin to decrease rapidly.

“It isn't like there's some heater in the deep ocean suddenly,” Swain says. “It's just that we've turned off the air conditioner and we're allowing the surface waters to warm.”

Kelvin waves can also help to raise sea levels along the California coast by “keeping the water from moving physically offshore,” Swain says. While Kelvin waves are imperceptible to the average person, their impacts aren’t.

Californians have been living through several weeks of intense coastal flooding and big waves enhanced by these higher sea levels. San Francisco and the surrounding area are under a coastal flood advisory through Friday morning, and waves have reached over 30 feet (9 meters) in height and even set off seismographs. (Another storm is set to hit the Bay Area this weekend.) It’s also contributing to heavier rainfall, with locations from San Francisco to Burbank setting hourly rainfall records in recent days.

But the warmer water itself is also contributing to this temporary sea level rise, thanks to simple physics: Warmer water takes up more space, helping push up sea levels.

The warm water is driving weather even more unprecedented than the intense storms. On Tuesday, two rare twin waterspouts formed over San Francisco Bay, the result of cold storm air moving over unusually warm waters. These phenomena are generally seen off the coast of Florida or the Mediterranean—not in the usually frigid waters of the Pacific.

“The air temperatures are somewhat winter-like right now, but the water ain't,” Swain says. “It’s an indicator that things aren’t as they usually are in this part of the world.”

#498. Rights court rules Turkey must release jailed lawmaker Atalay

The European Court of Human Rights has called for the release of imprisoned elected lawmaker Can Atalay. Atalay has been in prison for almost five years despite rulings from the Turkish Constitutional Court.

The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) ruled against Turkey over the detention of human rights lawyer and elected lawmaker Can Atalay.

The ECHR published its decision on Tuesday, saying that Turkey must release Atalay and allow him to take up his seat in the Turkish parliament.

The court ruled that his continued detention had been intended to silence him and undermine political pluralism.

It ordered Turkey to pay him €32,500 (about $35,700) in compensation.

The judges stressed that Atalay's case should not be considered separately, but rather in the wider context of the detention of political opponents, human rights activists and journalists in Turkey.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Turkey was among the original signatories of the European Convention on Human Rights. Yet it has previously refused to comply with the court's decisions in the cases of rights activist Osman Kavala and prominent Kurdish politician Selahattin Demirtas.

As a lawyer, Atalay represented victims in numerous social and political cases in Turkey, as well as in freedom of speech cases involving journalists and writers.

He was also among the leading voices in the 2013 Gezi protests, which the government called an attempted coup.

Because of his involvement in the protests, Atalay, along with seven others, was sentenced to 18 years in prison in April 2022 for "aiding and abetting an attempted coup."

Continuing his struggle from the infamous Silivri prison, Atalay ran as a candidate for the Workers' Party of Turkey (TIP) in the 2023 parliamentary elections.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A candidate for the earthquake-hit province of Hatay, he won his seat but was denied release despite multiple rulings by the Constitutional Court, Turkey's top court.

His parliamentary status was revoked in 2024, a decision the Constitutional Court later overturned. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's party stopped the opposition from formally reading the decision in parliament.

Although a year later an opposition lawmaker read the decision in parliament, Atalay remains in jail.

After the ECHR's ruling was published, TIP leader Erkan Bas took to social media to call for Atalay's release and the restoration of his parliamentary mandate.

#496. The Best Gifts for the Techie in Your Life (2026)

Techy gizmos make great stocking stuffers or Secret Santa gifts for friends, family, or coworkers. In fact, we've collected them in our comprehensive list of the Best 40 Techy Gifts under $100—that should give you plenty to parse through for impulse buys and stocking stuffers.

But this list is not that. These are the big tech products that really got us amped up—many of which launched this year. They're more expensive than what you'd buy for an acquaintance, but if you're looking for a big reaction on Christmas morning from your kids, spouse, or significant other, one of these should do the trick.

Updated November 2026: I've added the iPad Mini, Sonos Era 300, and the Lego Smart Play Star Wars Throne Room setup.

Oura has a lock on the world of smart rings, and we've been loving the latest model, which came out this July. Because the Ring 5 is smaller and more comfortable than before, WIRED reviewer Boutayna Chokrane says she often forgets she's even wearing it. That's crucial for something you're supposed to wear at all times, including while sleeping or during workouts. It's billed as a “proactive” health and fitness platform, giving you data on everything from sleep patterns to predictive blood pressure signals. It's likely not worth upgrading from the previous version, but for the fitness and health nut in your life who doesn't own one yet, the Oura Ring 5 is the best smart ring you can buy.

We already have smart speakers. We have iPads. We have digital photo frames (or, at least, your parents do). So, a dedicated device that serves merely as a digital calendar might seem superfluous. Maybe it is, but reviewer Nena Farrell absolutely swears by them. As someone with a busy family who struggles to sync our calendars, I get the appeal: a calendar on a larger screen in your kitchen or living room, visible to everyone who walks by, certainly sounds convenient. It's not just a list of events, either. It also has a meals page to plan and organize family dinners, plus tasks to keep everyone on top of chores. And this latest 15-inch model, the Skylight Calendar 2, is the best so far.

It's not only our favorite Keychron keyboard—it's the best overall keyboard you can buy. Launched in early 2026, this mechanical keyboard has a mid-century modern vibe, made of wood and metal. The 75 percent layout gives you everything you'll likely need in a compact size, with all the usual Keychron features, such as hot-swappable switches, double-shot keycaps, and the usual excellent build quality. Unlike other mechanical keyboards you may have tried, this one is low-profile, which means the travel distance on each key isn't quite as long, and it's designed for typing first and foremost. It's a great office companion, and it'll be a smoother transition if you're coming from a more generic rubber-dome model like an Apple Magic Keyboard.

The iPhone Duo might be the talk of the town, but the new iPad Mini is the more practical purchase. First of all, it doesn't require trading in the iPhone you're already familiar with to risk it on a first-generation product. It also isn't nearly as expensive if you already have a phone that you like. And what you get is easily the best small tablet money can buy. The deliciously vibrant OLED display is brighter and bigger than in the past, and if you opt for the nano-texture screen, it becomes the ultimate outdoor tablet. It might be a bit too expensive for a tablet of its size, but it just might be the ultimate travel companion for the right person.

This Sonos speaker is built different, quite literally. It’s made specifically with Dolby Atmos spatial audio in mind, with six speaker drivers pointed in multiple directions to spread out sound like no other home speaker can. Outside of Atmos, it’s an excellent stereo speaker that sounds crisp and detailed, and can connect with Sonos soundbars to make a full surround sound setup. —Harry Rabinowitz

You know what they say: If it ain't broke, don't fix it. The Logitech MX Master 3S has long been the most popular productivity mouse you can buy, so expectations for its successor were high. Thankfully, the MX Master 4 (9/10, WIRED Recommends) delivers without rocking the boat too much. There's now haptic support in the thumb rest, and you can press here to activate the virtual Actions Ring. You can customize the ring in the Logi Options+ app to launch apps, open websites, insert symbols, or even type text—the options are nearly endless.

It might not be worth upgrading from the MX Master 3 or 3S, especially since the polling rate hasn't changed, but the MX Master 4 has taken the reins as the go-to wireless mouse for serious office workers. If you know someone who would appreciate a mouse that not only offers great ergonomic support but also feels extremely high-quality in the hand, look no further.

For more ideas for home office products that make great gifts, check out our comprehensive guide to the Best Work-from-Home Gear.

Whether it's the Rabbit R1 or Humane Pin, AI hardware has been a big flop so far. But this year, we finally started to see devices that are actually interesting and potentially useful. WIRED contributor Christopher Null tried out all the new product category of AI notetaking devices, which can dictate, record, summarize, and translate seamlessly using large language models. Pocket was among the top recommendations. It magnetically attaches to the back of your phone and can even record phone calls without needing to keep it on speakerphone. Many AI notetakers require a paid subscription, while Pocket offers a substantial free option and only requires Pocket Pro as an upgrade for unlimited history.

With all the earbuds we review, you might think our audio experts are above something as common as AirPods. But Apple really nailed it this year with the AirPods Pro 3 (9/10, WIRED Recommends). It's been almost three years since Apple updated its noise-canceling earbuds, and the latest model adds a new ear tip design, supports real-time translation, and delivers vastly improved noise canceling and longer battery life. According to our testers, the earbuds last up to eight hours with noise canceling on, enough for more than a full day of work. All that makes this pair the best AirPods ever made.

GoPro has a new premium camera, and it's one of the most expensive action cameras you can buy. But our camera expert and outdoors enthusiast, Scott Gilbertson, says it's totally worth it. The new model, the GoPro Mission 1 Pro, has a larger 1-inch sensor than the Hero models, letting it shoot up to 8K at 60 fps. That might sound like overkill, but 8K lets you crop and zoom in on what you capture on your adventures while exporting to 4K without a big hit to image quality (unless you're fortunate enough to own an 8K TV). Scott also praises the new slow-motion mode, shooting up to 4K at 240 fps—even when zoomed in. The older GoPro Hero 13 Black is still a great option if you want to save some money, but the Mission 1 Pro's upgrade in image quality is noteworthy for a camera this small.

The best espresso machines cost well over $1,000 and take up your entire kitchen counter. They aren't exactly very “giftable.” The Breville Bambino challenges that assumption. It's only $300, yet it has many of the same features as more expensive machines, such as a thermoblock for instant heating. Of course, as a smaller, budget option, it's missing some things, such as automatic milk frothing. But according to former WIRED reviewer, Matthew Korfhage, pairing the Bambino with a solid grinder gives you “beautiful cups with counter space to spare.” Who wouldn't want that?

Smart Play is Lego's next big move into adding some serious tech into its classic brick-building. Despite looking like standard Legos, each Smart Brick has a custom chip, light array, speaker, and a variety of sensors. You can probably imagine how all this tech plays out in a set as immersive as the Star Wars Throne Room Duel. If you want to experience the latest in the world of Lego, it doesn't get more cutting-edge than this (even if our reviewer found that the tech took some of the magic away).

#494. U.S. officially loses measles elimination status amid ongoing outbreaks

The U.S. on Tuesday lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus.

The Pan American Health Organization announced the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country's epidemiological evidence. The director of PAHO, the regional branch of the World Health Organization, made the final call that measles is endemic — or always present — in the U.S. following 12 months of continuous transmission.

In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking new ones.

"The commission concluded that endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn — a recommendation which I have accepted," Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO director, said during a news briefing on Tuesday.

It's a devastating step backward for American public health, as declining childhood vaccination rates and vaccine hesitancy fuel outbreaks across the country that have sickened thousands of people and led to a tragic string of preventable deaths. Among the deaths where vaccination status was reported, all were unvaccinated.

More than 5,400 measles cases had been reported nationwide in 2026 as of mid-November, marking the country's worst outbreak in more than three decades. States have confirmed 10 deaths associated with the disease so far in 2026: seven in Pennsylvania, one in New York and two in Wisconsin.

The commission found that out of 52 U.S. states and territories it tracked, 48 experienced measles outbreaks during the reporting period between January 2025 and January 2026, PAHO Assistant Director Dr. Rhonda Sealey-Thomas said during the briefing. But Barbosa said the countries are already taking action to control outbreaks, such as strengthening vaccination, surveillance for timely case detection and outbreak response efforts.

The U.S. in particular has ramped up vaccination efforts to close immunity gaps, particularly in areas with low immunization coverage experiencing outbreaks, said Dr. Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO's Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization. He said PAHO expects the U.S. to present its corrective action plan in the coming weeks, outlining strategies to regain its designation.

In a Tuesday release, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said it will continue to ensure all communities have the resources to prevent and respond to outbreaks and is committed to working with states and other local partners to restore the U.S.'s measles elimination status.

CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said in the release that the measles elimination designation "is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does." She said the agency has invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach communities where transmission is occurring.

Last week, Schwartz told Reuters that the agency is going to be "doing the same exact thing that we've been doing today" if the U.S. loses its measles-free status.

The decision also poses a new test for the Trump administration and its Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has taken steps to change recommendations for the childhood measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine and has a long history of questioning its safety without evidence.

But Kennedy, in a Tuesday X post, said he continues to recommend MMR vaccination as "the most effective way to prevent measles."

"We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," Kennedy said. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment."

CNBC previously reported on how the return of measles in the U.S. exposes weaknesses in the nation's public health system that raise concerns about the return of other eliminated diseases. The resurgence of measles exposes eroding trust in health institutions and growing challenges in persuading people to protect themselves, their children and their communities.

Public health experts previously told CNBC that the return of measles ultimately boils down to fewer children getting vaccinated.

The MMR vaccine is about 97% effective against measles after two doses, while a single dose is 93% effective, according to the CDC. Yet data aggregated by the CDC shows that vaccination coverage for that shot among U.S. kindergarteners fell to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, which is below the 95% threshold public health officials generally recommend to prevent sustained transmission.

The American Medical Association urged the public to get vaccinated after PAHO's announcement.

"We must treat the current measles outbreaks as an urgent call to rebuild trust in science-based recommendations and restore strong, fully-funded public health infrastructure to protect families and communities and prevent the return of diseases once eliminated," AMA President Dr. Willie Underwood said in a statement.

In a separate statement, the pharmaceutical industry's largest lobbying group called on policymakers to provide "clear, accurate information about the seriousness of measles infection and the effectiveness of vaccines against it, restore and sustain high vaccination coverage in every community, strengthen vaccination efforts, and invest in disease surveillance and rapid outbreak response."

"We have the tools to eliminate measles again and what we need now is the commitment to use them," said Dr. Michael Ybarra, chief medical officer of the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America.

Measles isn't just a public health threat — it's also a huge financial burden on the healthcare system, CNBC reported.

Based on this year's case count, a new tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates an economic cost of nearly $83 million for the outbreaks. That total includes $56 million in public health response costs, almost $25 million in lost productivity and more than $1.8 million in direct medical expenses.

The U.S. now joins Canada, Spain and the U.K., which all recently lost their measles-free status after a review by experts at the World Health Organization. While the U.S. dropped out of the WHO, it remains a member of PAHO, its Americas branch.

#493. Yellowjackets: What is Melissas plan?!

If three seasons of Yellowjackets has taught us anything, it's that you don't mess with Shauna Shipman (aka Shauna Sadecki). Melissa learned that the hard way last season, when she sent a tape that put the Yellowjackets on her scent.

Shauna (Melanie Lynskey) didn't just find her, attack her, and bite off a bit of Melissa's arm. She also tried to feed it to her. Well, Season 4 of Yellowjackets came back with a vengeance, and so did Melissa (Hillary Swank).

Fresh from killing Van (Lauren Ambrose), Melissa begins episode 1 on the run with her wife, Alex (Jaylee Hamidi), and their child. In a grimy hotel room, she confesses to her partner the truth (or some of it). Her name is not Kelly, it's Melissa. She was a Yellowjacket. She was on the plane that crashed.

Melissa says she "rebooted her life" — which is a wild way to reframe faking your death. "I'm still the same person you married," she insists, "just with a different name and way, way shittier past than I told you about on our first date."

Then this conversation reveals something huge:

Alex responds to Melissa's partial confession with: "My mom was out there. She's the one who called for help. She's the reason they got rescued. "

So, there were signs last season about how Tai (Jasmin Savoy Brown), Van (Liv Hewson), Shauna (Sophie Nélisse), and Misty (Samantha Hanratty) talked about Hannah (Ashley Sutton) that suggested she didn't make it out of the Yellowjackets camp alive. Alex's revelation further cements that Hannah died out there. When Alex asks her wife if she met her mom out there, Melissa lies, "No. I didn't know her."

Melissa goes on to say that it was because she wish she'd known Hannah that she moved to the late scientist's hometown to start over. "Maybe I could create a life in her honor," she says. That might be true. But even as Melissa comes clean, she's still lying to Alex. And by sharing any of this, Melissa could be putting Alex in danger from the others. At least she's honest about that.

The episode begins with the Yellowjackets in a Canadian hospital, seeing their injuries tended to. But there's no sign of Hannah.

As the Yellowjackets share their story of survival with authorities, they all recite the exact same story:

"The plane crashed. Our friends died. And the rest of starved and scavenged and prayed until they finally found us."

They claim to have no knowledge of the missing frog scientists. To cover their tracks, they let the adults assume Hannah made the distress call. So, Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) never gets proper credit for her heroics there.

How Hannah died, however, is still a mystery.

After the scene of Melissa's confession to her wife, a title card says four weeks have passed. Shauna is acting out in her frustration, lashing out at a convenience store clerk and a stinky detective, the latter of whom has lost any trace of Melissa and her family.

Cut to: Melissa and Alex setting up in a newly leased home — which is right next door to the Sadecki household. Alex seems nervous about the plan, as Melissa assures, "Hey, we can't run forever."

Then, Melissa confronts Shauna by showing up at her door with a "Hi" and a bottle of wine. To this, Shauna says, "Well, this was very stupid... You moved in next door to me. Now I know where you are."

Melissa responds, "Yeah, and everyone else will too," just as a news van pulls up behind her!

In the wilderness and in the present timeline, Melissa knows full well how Shauna's rage can result in violence, sometimes deadly violence.

However, she also knows Shauna is strategic and a survivor. By staying in plain sight, Melissa thinks Shauna will be powerless to hurt her, because to do so would bring fresh attention to the Yellowjackets and their past.

Is she right? We'll can't wait to find out.

#492. Back to 1997: Russia wants NATO to roll back its eastern expansion

The Kremlin is reportedly calling on NATO to withdraw from large parts of Eastern Europe. What this would mean for the security of millions of Europeans — and what lies behind Russia's plan.

During talks on ending the war in Ukraine, Russian representatives in Abu Dhabi presented a document containing far-reaching demands, The New York Times reports.

Dated November 10, the document reportedly calls not only for an end to Western arms deliveries to Ukraine but also for NATO to withdraw its troops and bases and move them back to where they were in 1997.

The year 1997 refers to the NATO alliance before its first eastward expansion, according to the Kremlin. At the time, NATO had 16 members. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary had already been invited to join but did not formally become members of the defense alliance until two years later. In the following years, more countries in Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe joined, followed most recently by countries in Scandinavia. Today, NATO has 32 member states in Europe and North America.

According to the report, Russia is not explicitly demanding that Central and Eastern European countries leave, but rather that the NATO alliance end its military presence in those countries.

A withdrawal of NATO troops and bases from member states that joined the alliance after 1997 would significantly weaken their defense capabilities. For example, since 2004, NATO allies, including Germany, have taken turns policing the airspace over Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

Because the Baltic states do not have fighter jets of their own for independent air policing, NATO provides the capability. Since 2026, the mission has been part of a broader air defense presence. The planned deployment of the German Lithuania Brigade, which is expected to be fully operational by the end of 2027, would also have to be halted.

In Romania, meanwhile, the Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base near Constanța on the Black Sea is currently being expanded. Once completed, it is set to become Europe's largest NATO air base by area — even larger than Ramstein in Germany.

"Under no circumstances will we allow anyone to establish new security rules for this part of the world over the heads of Poland and Europe," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told TVP World. His Bulgarian counterpart, Rumen Radev, called a NATO withdrawal "unthinkable and unrealistic." No country should be forced by external pressure to reverse its decision on which alliance to join.

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal also rejected any Russian say in changes to Europe's security order: "We have nothing to discuss with Russia about Europe's security order; it is working well."

The strong rejection from the capitals of NATO's eastern members, however, masks fears along the alliance's eastern flank that a deal between Washington and Moscow could turn their security into a bargaining chip.

In the event of an armed attack on a NATO member, the other alliance members are obligated under Article 5 to come to its aid. Each member decides for itself what measures it considers necessary, which may include the use of military force.

For the mutual defense commitment to deter a potential aggressor, that country must believe NATO can intervene militarily quickly and effectively in a crisis. The deployment of allied troops along the eastern flank serves precisely this purpose. A withdrawal would make defense more difficult and could lead Russia to believe that an attack on NATO territory would involve fewer risks for Moscow.

As part of their security framework, European countries have agreed that states are free to decide which alliances they wish to join. NATO points to Article 10 of its founding treaty, which enshrines its open-door policy for European countries. The 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act also explicitly stated that neither side had the right to veto the other's decisions.

Back in November 1990, the participating states of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE), including the Soviet Union, had already agreed in the Charter of Paris to respect each country's freedom to choose its own security arrangements.

During the negotiations surrounding German reunification, then-US Secretary of State James Baker and German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher used language that suggested putting limits on NATO's eastward expansion.

Their remarks came during discussions about unified Germany's membership in NATO and the possible deployment of NATO forces on the territory of the former East Germany. However, no written, legally binding general promise was ever agreed that NATO would never expand to include other former Warsaw Pact countries.

In the 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act, both sides declared that they no longer considered each other adversaries. NATO stated that, under the security conditions prevailing at the time and in the foreseeable future, it intended to ensure its collective defense through reinforcement rather than the additional permanent stationing of "substantial combat forces." The agreement explicitly gave Moscow no veto over NATO decisions.

In the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, Russia, the United States and the United Kingdom reaffirmed their commitment to respect Ukraine's independence and existing borders and to refrain from the use of force. These assurances were linked to Ukraine's decision to give up its nuclear weapons. However, the memorandum did not oblige the United States or the United Kingdom to defend Ukraine militarily in the event of an attack. NATO membership was not addressed at the time.

Just over two months before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin presented two draft treaties to the United States and NATO. In them, Russia demanded an end to further NATO enlargement. The draft agreement with NATO also proposed that Russia and NATO members that had already joined the alliance as of May 27, 1997, refrain from deploying additional troops or weapons on the territory of other European countries beyond the levels stationed there on that date.

Security guarantees for the postwar period and a future security framework for Europe were also on the agenda in Abu Dhabi. Negotiating NATO troop deployments and alliance enlargement alongside an end to the war in Ukraine would give Moscow additional leverage. Russia has long maintained that the "root causes" of the war must be addressed. The Kremlin includes NATO enlargement and the alliance's military presence in Eastern Europe among those causes.

So far, no significant Western player has expressed willingness to accept Russia's demands in Abu Dhabi. On the contrary, former Polish intelligence coordinator Stanislaw Zaryn viewed the talks as an attempt to buy time and weaken the West ahead of another confrontation.

This article was originally published in German.

#490. Yellowjackets cliffhanger: What did Natalie see?

A lot goes down in Yellowjackets' Season 4 premiere! The team returns to civilization in the past timeline. Meanwhile, in the present, Misty (Christina Ricci) is plotting to kill Shauna (Melanie Lynskey), while Melissa's (Hilary Swank) looking to outwit the former Antler Queen with a big move.

And yet that's not the cliffhanger that the premiere episode goes out on.

Instead, the first episode of Season 4 takes us back to the wilderness, right after Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) has successfully called for help using the frog scientists' SAT phone.

She races back to camp, shouting, "It worked! We're getting rescued." But as she reaches the team's shelters, she stops in her tracks, and says, "What the fuck?" as she looks at...something.

At the end of Season 3, Natalie conspired with Misty (Samantha Hanratty), Hannah (Ashley Sutton), and Van (Liv Hewson) to sneak away during the hunt, so she could call for help. This means Natalie wasn't present when Mari (Alexa Barajas) became Pit Girl, or for the feast that follows. The following morning is when Shauna (Sophie Nélisse) realizes Hannah has been wearing Natalie's garb to hide her absence from the ritual.

So, option one is that Natalie, who ran back to the camp not with joy but determination, was hoping to stop the hunt with the news. But she arrived to find Mari like the frog scientists had found Coach Ben (Steven Krueger): ritualistically slaughtered and cut to pieces.

Option 2 relates to the episode's opening credits. Season after season, Yellowjackets has teased details of future episodes through imagery in the title sequence. In the premiere episode, those images included an image of Teen Shauna lying on her back in the snow, badly beaten.

At the end of Season 3, Shauna was furiously crying out to know where Natalie had gone. The answer was to the mountains to use the SAT phone. So, did something happen in the camp between that moment and Nat's return that results in her shocked expression at the end of episode 1? There's only way to find out. #489. Regular Tech Bros Are Worried About Honeypots

When the founder of a cybersecurity firm hired Blaine Anderson as a matchmaker, it wasn’t just because the man was lonely. It was also, Anderson says, because he was “super worried about spies.”

The cybersecurity founder isn’t the only one. As Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security dominates headlines and AI companies reportedly warn employees against “honeypots,” matchmakers say that more men with pretty normal lives are worried that their dates may have ulterior motives: accessing corporate secrets.

“Even if you're not a CEO or at a big tech giant, these fears have trickled down to just regular professionals,” Simone Grossman, a Brooklyn-based matchmaker, tells WIRED.

One tech worker, who requested anonymity in order to speak candidly, says he considers himself “highly selective” about the people he interacts with face-to-face.

“Even though I could vet you from looking you up online, I can't help but still be a tad dubious,” he tells WIRED. On a scale from zero to 10, with 10 being the most anxious about espionage, he puts himself at a seven.

Even though the vast majority of tech employees likely won’t be targeted for romantic espionage, matchmakers say more clients have lately expressed concerns about women exploiting them for their corporate secrets. One Palantir employee told Andersen he wouldn’t date anyone who was a Chinese or Russian national. The anxiety has even become a marketing opportunity: One company is pitching its new line of AI executive girlfriends as a “zero espionage” alternative to human dating.

The concern isn’t entirely without basis. Some companies hire consultants to advise executives and lower-level employees with access to sensitive information on security risks, including the possibility of honeypots. Several of these consultants tell WIRED that raising the subject can be awkward.

“This one is always a very difficult message to deliver—to explain to, say, very sensitive engineers that maybe they're getting a lot of email attention because of their job,” says Isaac Stone Fish, founder and chief executive of the business intelligence firm Strategy Risks, “as opposed to the charm and force of their personality.”

Amy Andersen, founder of Silicon Valley matchmaking company Linx Dating (and no relation to Blaine Anderson), says that for clients concerned about their romantic partners’ intentions, she offers background checks, personal vetting, and NDAs. The security features are part of her “bespoke” packages that range anywhere from $75,000 to more than $500,000 for the “Founders Level.”

The anxiety is particularly acute among AI workers, whose net worths—and therefore their perceived romantic desirability—are on the rise.

“If you're somebody who is a little bit shy or who is maybe a very stereotypical engineer type, to suddenly have your market value in the dating world change so drastically—you're already suspicious,” Grossman says.

To be worried about corporate espionage on top of all that, she says, is “a mind fuck.”

Honeypots and their state or corporate sponsors often look for “signs of vulnerability, such as an unhappy marriage, or someone seeking “excitement or adventure,” says Ira Winkler, a security consultant and the chief information security officer in residence at identity protection company Cloaked. Lonely people are opportune targets, regardless of marriage or relationship status.

The advice security experts give is somewhat obvious: If it seems too good to be true, it probably is.

“Really, if a beautiful woman approaches you, you know it's not for your personality,” Winkler tells his clients.

When tech workers do think of honeypots, they may gravitate toward the stereotype of a beautiful stranger who seduces someone at a bar and then extracts company secrets. “Any time one of us would take a trip to Asia, someone would always make a comment about getting a foreign girlfriend, or future wife, etc.,” one tech worker tells WIRED about his experience at a majority-male workplace. “We'd joke about them meeting a spy, but nobody really considered that seriously. Mostly they were just thinking of sex.”

That setup is largely a misconception. In reality, according to Greg Rinckey, founding partner of the legal services and consulting firm Tully Rinckey, most honeypot victims are groomed over time. “We’re talking sometimes months, could be years, where they're fostering that relationship,” he says. Rinckey compares it to scammers trying to keep victims on the phone: The longer someone talks to another person and feels they know them, the more likely they are to trust them with sensitive information.

Catherine Marinis-Yaqub, a principal at the crisis and security consulting group Control Risks, tells WIRED that when people imagine the beautiful stranger at a bar, they may miss more likely scenarios, like an unexpected guest at a business meeting, a savvy networker at an industry conference, or a flirt at someone’s favorite coffee shop. Jensen Huang met Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese asset, for example, through a mutual business associate (who, according to The Wall Street Journal, also happened to be Alice’s husband).

For the man too scared of spies to make contact with a human romantic partner, there’s always artificial intelligence.

On Tuesday, in the wake of the Huang scandal, AI-relationship platform Joi AI launched a suite of "zero espionage" Executive Girlfriends. Brand director Julie Levin describes Joi AI as a “safe space” for exploration, where users can exchange NSFW texts, images, and videos with AI companions without judgment or rejection.

It made sense, she says, to extend that sense of security to honeypot-phobia.

“If they have some business secrets they don't want to share on a date or they feel nervous discussing with real people,” Levin says, “they can discuss them comfortably with their AIs.” (Levin assures WIRED that Joi AI employs several layers of security and that all of the data is anonymized.)

High-profile executives are among those most at risk of honeypots, says Winkler, the security consultant. They can also be some of the hardest to protect.

“It's really hard to influence somebody who's in control of the company and just happens to be a sleazebag,” Winkler says.

It’s particularly difficult, says Rinckey, when bosses think they’re the smartest person in the room and consider themselves immune to manipulation. It’s also not easy, he says, to be in the position of challenging an executive.

“Cocky, arrogant, and boisterous” chief executives make for desirable targets because “they love to talk about their business, and they love to talk about themselves,” Rinckey says. In these situations, he says, “you don't even really have to pry them that much.”

#488. Yellowjackets Season 4 soundtrack: Every needle drop you need to know

As the story of a soccer team gone cannibal kicks off in 1996, Yellowjackets has plumbed the depths of '90s music to make one banger soundtrack season after season. This year, if you're looking to play (or headbang) along, we've got you covered with the needle drops of Season 4 as each episode hits.

But that's not all. Sure, you can use this collection to built a killer playlist. (Buzz, buzz!) We're also going to dive into a bit of what it means and why each song might have been selected for its particular Yellowjackets moment.

Let's kick things off with the Season 4 premiere:

Sample lyric: If I could find that Heina / And that Sancho that she's found / Well, I'd pop a cap in Sancho / And I'd slap her down

Season 4 opens with this hit song that had a total chokehold on teens in 1996. The lyrics sing of a hapless dude making messy decisions.

Fittingly, it plays while teen Jeff (Jack DePew) is getting high on the job at Taylor's Furniture Store with his doofy bestie Randy (Riley Baron). Despite some violent lyrics, "Santeria" is a upbeat tune that speaks to Jeff's laid-back attitude, post-graduation.

But once he sees the news of the Yellowjackets rescue on TV, the theme song cuts in and dramatically changes the episode's tone.

Sample lyric: It was cool / Nothing fire / Nothing broke / Keep simple / Nothing tired / Nothing old / Same as you / Same as you

For four seasons now, this song's cryptic lyrics have played as a pitch-perfect distillation of the show's female rage, rooted in lust, jealousy, and even love.

Sample lyric: My girl, my girl, don't lie to me / Tell me, where did you sleep last night?In the pines, in the pines / Where the sun don't ever shine / I would shiver the whole night through

After the opening credits, Yellowjackets picks up with the titular team in a hospital, where they are safe but look worried, likely about the world learning how it is they made it through their ordeal.

Playing over the sequence is Kurt Cobain's cover of the American folk song also known as "In the Pines," which is recognized as a murder ballad. The lyrics reflect a haunting story of homicide in the woods. The particular song has been covered by a variety of acts since its creation in the 1870s, including the father of Bluegrass Bill Monroe, Blues singer Lead Belly, and Dolly Parton.

Cobain famously covered the song on his MTV Unplugged appearance, on Nov. 18, 1993. So, it's a cover the Yellowjackets themselves might recognize. Moreover, his grunge rendition reflects the trauma and terror of the team's return to civilization.

Sample lyric: For the life of me, I cannot remember / What made us think that we were wise and we'd never compromise / For the life of me, I cannot believe / We'd ever die for these sins, we were merely freshmen

This '90s song plays in the present timeline, but in a meaningful way. Showing up to Shauna's (Melanie Lynskey) door in episode 1, Melissa (Hilary Swank) presents a bottle of wine along with the news that she's moved in next door, and that she's called the press. Shauna looks on in shock asking, "What did you do?" as "The Freshmen" plays.

From 1997, this hit song from the Verve Pipe tells the tale of two young men, reflecting on the damage they've done to a shared lover. In this context, "The Freshmen" plays as if Shauna's subconscious is making an excuse ("we were merely freshmen").

Or perhaps, this song's use use here is meant to reflect Melissa's perspective. As the wounded lover, her story could show what might happen if that lover struck back with the poetic justice of reclaiming her narrative and her future.

#486. The Smart Ring Goes to Church

Stressed? Heart rate elevated? If you’re wearing a smart ring from Oura, Ultrahuman, or Samsung, the spike could prompt app suggestions like breathing exercises, meditations, or a physical reset like a short walk. So far, so Silicon Valley. But now you can add reading the Bible to that list of self-soothing activities.

The first generation of Christian smart rings is here, joining other religious wearables like iQibla’s dedicated Muslim smartwatches, rings, and Hajj bands alongside “kosher” smartwatch apps. Two new devices in particular—Glorify’s Ring and Everblessed Technology’s Elah Ring—connect to hugely popular Christian prayer apps with tens of millions of users, and both claim to be the world’s first Christian smart ring.

Both are first, in their own ways. Everblessed’s $249 Elah Ring S1 went on sale in October and is shipping in the US. The $299 Glorify Ring launched in July, with reservations open and shipping set for January 2027, but 77,000 units of an earlier beta iteration, the Amen Ring made by faith tech company ConfideIn (which merged with Glorify this May), were given away last Christmas. Everblessed manages the Blessed app, and Glorify has an eponymous app.

Another big player in prayer apps is Hallow, aimed at Catholics, backed by Vice President JD Vance’s Narya venture capital firm and celebrity ambassadors, with 24 million installs to date. Hallow’s toe-dip into wearables was a 2024 smart rosary with NFC embedded in the crucifix, made with Italian brand Ghirelli; Everblessed tried an earbud, necklace, and bedside device before settling on the ring design.

Head-to-head on design, the Elah and Glorify rings are both made from titanium alloy, with a thorn-inspired twist for Glorify and a minimalist band featuring a cross for the Elah S1, which is also IP68 waterproof to 5 meters.

For now, the Elah Ring is slightly techier: prayer reminders come via the cross, which glows via an LED, and “gentle” vibrations; these can pulse at certain times of day or be triggered by changes in heart rate and stress levels, picked up by a photoplethysmography (PPG) sensor. Glorify’s CEO Henry Costa tells WIRED these emotion-based reminders will land on the Glorify Ring in six months; for now, you can set the times of day you want prayer reminders, track heart rate, blood oxygen, stress, and sleep via the optical sensor.

One addition to the Glorify Ring that Costa says he personally uses “a lot” is recording prayers straight into the built-in mic. The ring has a light to signal when it's recording, and the app transcribes them. Everblessed CEO Ricky Xia says that, after consulting with pastors and users, the feeling was that voice notes on the ring were seen as “suspicious.” It’s available in-app, but most people don’t pray out loud, and too many features drain the battery life. (The Elah Ring runs for up to six days on one charge; Glorify for four to five days.)

Both companies see the smart ring nudges helping wearers prioritize meaningful quiet time, away from screens, while offering in-app Christian practices as an alternative to Eastern meditation. Glorify offers Bible study, courses, and meditations. Blessed has devotional “anchors,” Bible texts and audio, plus guided breathing. Xia says he’s happy if the Elah vibrates and a user picks up a paper Bible rather than the Blessed app, while Costa says he’s “crying out to use my phone less.”

Both Glorify (founded in 2020, now merged with ConfideIn and headquartered in the San Francisco Bay Area) and Blessed (founded in 2023 and based in San Jose) operate in more than 150 countries. Perhaps the biggest difference between the two rings is their relationship to AI.

Xia is all-in, describing the S1 as an “AI-native” product, with a pastor-complementing, not-replacing FaithMate chatbot in the Blessed app, customized based on preferences, congregation, and depth of learning. ChatGPT is like a “good coworker,” he says, while FaithMate is designed to be “your friend” and an agent that can also handle secular tasks.

Costa is more circumspect, treading carefully on the consumer-facing side and noting that the Pope has weighed in with a 6,000-word encyclical on AI. A launch interview with CBN News garnered negative comments: “AI is Antichrist Information,” for one.

“The stance I’ve always taken is that our daily devotional is hand-authored by a team of theologians,” Costa says. “It’s prayed over, and that is a stamp of approval.” He criticizes AI slop prayer apps as inauthentic. Still, he says the Glorify team has already tested “many forms” of AI personalization: “Any time, if we do use AI, it must be very clear to the user.”

Smart ring owners were finding ways to add faith features to mainstream accessories before these rings came to fruition. For 20 years, timer and reminder apps have helped with prayer schedules, but recent examples are more creative. Heidi Campbell, professor of communication in religious studies at Texas A&M, refers to these DIY upgrades to the Oura ring and devices like the Muse headband as “spiritual mind-body hacking.”

Oura owners on #christiantiktok chat about how they already use the ring’s stress and HR alerts as a prompt to pause and reflect, as per Elah.

Smart ring users flag changes in resting heart rate and sleep quality with scripture following their daily practice. “It’s really helpful for, like, what was inhibiting me from getting to a meditative or contemplative prayer state?” Campbell says. “It takes some of the mystery out of prayer, I think, but that can also be positive. There is a way to do prayer well and not well.” Ring hackers can also dig into health stats during Lent, Ramadan, and Yom Kippur to analyze energy expenditure and how fasting periods affect their bodies.

The connected Christian ring is likely to remain niche, but that doesn’t mean the products will flop. James Stables, head of communications at smart ring manufacturer Ultrahuman, notes that attaching Christian practices to a trending category feels like a smart play. “Like prayer beads, the ring is analog in its on-body form and kind of tactile and haptic," he says.

AI-powered voice recordings and emerging attempts at emotion tracking are part of a new phase for smart rings, says Ekta Mittal, a senior analyst of connected devices at CCS Insight. These new “purpose-driven” features extend wearable tech into “new parts of consumers’ daily routines,” Mittal says. She suggests that while Glorify and Everblessed will add value for some, the rings are “not directly competing” with established smart ring giants like Oura, Ultrahuman, and Samsung.

The pandemic sped up the digital transition of many places of worship when congregations could not meet up in person, encouraging experimentation with social media. So it’s early days for Silicon Valley’s impact on organized religion. Researchers at the University of Würzburg in Germany, led by Ilona Nord, are studying the theological implications of using tech, including smart rings, for spiritual practices, investigating which values are baked into secular devices and apps.

Campbell suggests many Christian groups haven’t stopped to consider the unintentional consequences of cultivating spirituality via personal tech. “All of these things are about individualizing the practice, which is good, but the challenges are for religions which are really focused on communal aspects,” she says. Not everyone has the money or connectivity to access these gadgets, but also, more existentially, “it puts spiritual development over communal development.”

Xia points to the Blessed app’s communities, including its Healing Room broadcast feature, which lets pastors go live with sermons. It's not in the Elah app yet, but it's on the roadmap. Costa says communal practice is a core pillar, highlighting the “social layer” of public notes made on Christian texts in-app and an upcoming Glorify Ring feature which will allow a user to pair their device with a family member’s ring: “When your loved one is feeling down, you’ll get a buzz to check in with them.”

#484. Yellowjackets Season 4: What clues are hiding in the opening credits?

Yellowjackets is back. With Season 4 comes new mysteries and new opening title cards inviting viewers to speculate on what's next. With each episode, Mashable will be probing these details, looking for questions and their answers. So, buckle up.

The theme song, "No Return" by Craig Wedren and Anna Waronker, roars to life over VHS footage once more. Some images are classic, like pre-crash footage of the team smiling and Jackie (Ella Purnell) smirking on the soccer pitch and drawing a threatening finger across her neck. But others are new.

In Season 4, Episode 1, here are all the curious images we noticed:

Melanie Lynskey is shown wide-mouthed before a microphone, suggesting adult Shauna has something to say (or sing?) in Season 4. Considering Shauna has a special skill for brutal one-liners, whoever she's looking at should be trembling.

Under blood and a prosthetic broken nose, Sophie Nélisse is hard to recognize in the moment. But freeze-frame the credits, and there's no doubt that's Teen Shauna. She's lying in the snow. So, presumably this is still when the girls were in the wilderness.

At the end of the Season 3, Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) successfully reached the outside world through the frog scientist's SAT phone. So, what happens before rescue comes?

The colors of this shot are brighter and more saturated than Yellowjackets tends to go. The uniform is a throwback 1950s style, and actress Tawny Cypress is smiling in a wide-eyed way that's not in keeping with Taissa's character. So, we're speculating this will be another dream sequence or vision. This one feel Lynchian, and as his work touches on doomed romances and the dark underbelly of suburbia, one can assume he'd speak to Taissa on both levels. But what does it mean?

Her face is covered by a mask, but there's no mistaking her frizzy blond hair and glasses. Will the girls' return to civilization show Misty's path to working at the old folks home? Or will this be a dream sequence where she imagines what her future might be?

In the credits, it's a close-up of what appears to be Shauna, wearing a blindfold and holding a string. To get a fuller context, you have to look to the sneak peek images Paramount released on Nov. 5.

Here you can see she's holding a knife on a string while standing inside the crashed plane, her team huddled on the floor around her. This recalls the ritual seance the girls did in Season 1 in the cabin's attic. They'd tried to contact the presumed dead owner of the cabin, and instead tapped into something darker and more mysterious.

The swinging knife is meant to answer the girls' questions. So, are they calling on the "it" of the wilderness for advice ahead of their rescue?

Whose head is being pried open in this nightmarish way? It's hard to tell from the close-up, which gives away no facial features. Dark hair and a sleeve ending in lace are the only clues. But based on the outrageousness, we're going to guess this one is a nightmare within the show.

This set dressing was spotted by fans on Reddit eight months back. But what's its role in the show? Well, we know Jackie's parents have money. Could this be how they memorialize their golden girl?

That's probably bad news for Shauna, right?

Christina Ricci's been a violent ax-wielder before. (We remember Lizzie Borden Took an Ax and The Lizzie Borden Chronicles). We also know an ax is how Edwin died last season — though by Lottie's hand. Yet despite Misty's maniacal facial expression, and her still wearing Natalie's leather jacket, we're guess this is more a Misty-to-the-rescue moment. Maybe she's about to pull a Shining and ax a door?

As this is shot comes from the opening scene of Season 4, there's not much mystery here. Teen Jeff (Jack DePew) had moved on from Shauna and Jackie, getting high with Randy (Riley Baron) and working at Jackie's parents' furniture story. Then he sees her face on the news, with reports of their rescue.

With Shauna finally coming back from the wilderness, we're likely to see how grief and love brought these two together for a marriage we may not envy, but kind of admire?

#483. FAA pauses installation of new routers after ground stop

The Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday it would pause the installation of new routers after problems with the technology led the agency to issue a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours. It was the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control.

The Wall Street Journal first reported the news about the pause.

The FAA and Department of Transportation have said L3Harris was working to convert the communications network from copper wires to fiber optic.

Democratic members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation this week asked the FAA and the Department of Transportation for clarity on what went wrong.

"Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed," the senators wrote in a statement. "Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety."

The agencies have said they are working to figure out the root cause of the issue and have reiterated that there is no indication of a cyberattack or outside threat.

The senators also asked for a briefing with the FAA, L3Harris and Juniper Networks, which is making the new devices, by Monday. They asked the companies to lay out why the operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy and answer other questions about what led to the outage.

CNBC has reached out to L3Harris and Juniper Networks for comment.

Duffy on Friday called for Congress to approve $50 billion in funding for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system, more than he has previously asked for. Democratic lawmakers pushed back on the request, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.

Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday that he thinks there will be support for air traffic control modernization, but that the allocation should be specifically for safety upgrades.

"I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded," he said. "Some of that is not safety related, but we just discussed there, and what I expressed is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization."

Duffy dismissed the idea that the router issue had to do with the introduction of artificial intelligence tools and said it was "completely unfounded" because the AI system is not in communication with the defective router. He added that the FBI is helping to investigate the root cause of the issue.

Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have for years angered airline executives, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions.

— CNBC's Phil LeBeau, Leslie Josephs and Justin Papp contributed to this report.

#480. Hashim Thaci's second conviction in The Hague reignites debate in Kosovo about justice and the Kosovo Specialist Chambers

Former President Hashim Thaci has been convicted of trying to influence witnesses in his war crimes trial. The conviction has reignited debate in Kosovo about the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, the court that convicted him.

A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.

This term will be added to his 25-year sentence for war crimes, which was handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16.

According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility in The Hague with confidential information about witnesses in his war crimes trial and had instructed them on how to influence their testimony.

Three other men — former head of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency Bashkim Smakaj, former Minister of Justice Hajredin Kuci, and Fadil Fazliu — were also convicted.

Thaci, who was the former political leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War, is viewed by many in his home country as a hero. His war crimes conviction in September was greeted in Kosovo with anger and dismay.

Thaci has vowed to appeal the war crimes conviction.

His two convictions touch deep sensitivities in Kosovo society. Tuesday's ruling brings renewed attention to the war that ended 27 years ago, the role played by its former leaders, and the continuing debate over justice, individual or collective responsibility for the KLA's war to liberate Kosovo from Serbia, and trust in judicial institutions.

The response from the government of Kosovo was swift.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, the government said, "Trust in justice is built not only on the decisions that are made, but also on the manner in which they are reached. Therefore, our commitment to the rule of law and our insistence on the full respect of rights and procedural guarantees are part of the same principled position: Justice must not only be done, but must also be fair, transparent, and credible."

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was established in 2015 by the parliament of Kosovo at the instigation of the European Union and the United States.

The court was created to investigate serious crimes allegedly committed by members of the KLA during and after the Kosovo War.

For security reasons, including concerns about witness intimidation, the court was located in The Hague in the Netherlands.

After Thaci and three others were convicted of war crimes in first instance in September, Kosovo's state authorities established a working group to draft a strategy regarding the appeal proceedings before the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The group is chaired by Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca and includes members of Kosovo's parliament.

Prime Minister Albin Kurti has stated that the working group continues to believe that "the first-instance judgment of the Specialist Chambers is unjust, both legally and morally," and that as a result, "the government is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers."

In addition, the parliament of Kosovo is currently considering amendments to the law governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The draft law, which is expected to be adopted, envisages narrowing the court's mandate in several areas, including the time period covered by its jurisdiction, limiting the maximum prison sentence to 15 years, allowing sentences to be served in Kosovo, and introducing the possibility of presidential pardons for persons convicted by final court decisions.

How do political analysts and legal experts view the parliament's attempt to amend the law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers before the judicial process involving the four men convicted of war crimes has reached a final verdict?

"From an international perspective, at first glance, this initiative could even be interpreted as an attempt to interfere in the judicial process," said political analyst and university professor Artan Muhaxheri.

"Precisely for this reason, it is essential that Kosovo's political spectrum and its legal experts demonstrate beyond any doubt that this measure does not conflict with Kosovo's international obligations toward the European Union," Muhaxheri told DW, adding that this is the only way to ensure that the desired outcome is achieved and that the initiative does not produce the opposite effect.

"Issues relating to jurisdiction, statutory limits on maximum sentences, and other similar matters must be argued professionally and rigorously, demonstrating that they fully guarantee judicial independence and enjoy solid support within Kosovo's legal system, the same legal system that, first and foremost, established the Specialist Chambers," he said.

Ehat Miftaraj, executive director of the Kosovo Law Institute (IKD), told DW that although the Kosovo Specialist Chambers were established by the Republic of Kosovo itself, "the way the judicial process has unfolded has created the impression that judges, prosecutors and certain international actors have treated not only the accused but also Kosovo itself with distrust, prejudice, and an often condescending approach."

Miftaraj went on to say that reactions and objections in Kosovo to the decisions of the Specialist Chambers are also interpreted and judged in the historical and emotional context of the war and what Kosovo's citizens experienced during and after it.

"In a democratic society, every citizen, including political and institutional representatives, has the right to criticize judicial decisions," he said. "However, there is a fundamental distinction between criticism based on legal arguments and attempts to delegitimize courts or exert influence over judicial proceedings. And here, there is room for criticism of both sides."
